content.title: A Holistic Energy Governance Framework
content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition

content.text: Lesson 3 Overview

This lesson introduces a practical governance framework that connects core governance principles (like participation, transparency, and oversight) to key elements of the energy transition, such as infrastructure, finance, and social impacts. Using Nigeria’s experience as an example, we explore how this framework helps identify gaps, align institutions, and ensure no one is left behind.

Energy transition commitments and policies may have far-reaching effects across society, requiring collaboration among multiple stakeholders at various levels. While discussions around what a green transition entails have advanced, there appears to be less clarity on how it should be governed effectively ) (UNDP, 2023)

A well-structured governance framework is essential to ensure inclusivity, equity, and sustainability in the energy transition. This framework is built upon four key focus areas, which serve as foundational pillars for strengthening governance systems:

Each of these focus areas will be examined separately in the next chapter. However, before doing so, it is essential to consider how they should be approached.
UNDP’s experience in governance across more than 130 countries over decades has shown that success depends on four key approaches:

This framework is structured as a matrix (See the next page), combining the four focus areas discussed earlier (X-axis) and Four Elements of Energy Transition (Y-Axis). These represent the key areas where governance plays a role in energy transitions:

content.body: Political Vision & Commitment – Establishing long-term strategies and leadership for the transition.
Financial Capital & Investment – Mobilizing clean energy financing and ensuring financial transparency.
System Infrastructure & Innovation – Expanding renewable energy grids, technologies, and innovation.
Social Impacts & Equity – Managing job losses, reskilling, and social protection in the transition

content.text:
Each intersection in the matrix highlights a guiding question that helps assess the governance needs and implications for a fair energy transition.

By mapping these governance principles to energy transition elements, the framework helps identify gaps, risks, and opportunities in how a country manages its just energy transition 💬️.

Nigeria’s energy sector faces significant challenges in transitioning towards a sustainable energy future. Despite being rich in natural resources such as crude oil, natural gas, and coal (Brittanica 2025), the country struggles with widespread energy poverty, low electricity access, and deep-rooted governance fragmentation.
Electricity access is uneven, with only 60% of the population having access to electricity, dropping to 26% in rural areas. Meanwhile, over 74 million rural Nigerians remain disconnected from the grid (World Bank, 2023). Simultaneously, more than 90% of Nigeria’s exports rely on fossil fuels, despite the oil sector employing only 0.03% of the workforce (NEITI, 2019).

In response, the government introduced the Energy Transition Plan (ETP) in 2021. It enacted the Electricity Act in 2023, aiming to decentralize energy governance 💬️ and scale up renewable investment (Federal Government of Nigeria, 2021).
However, governance gaps have emerged in the implementation of this plan, including:

content.body: Fragmented leadership and weak institutional coordination, with ministries and agencies working in silos;
Conflicting policies that undermine long-term transition goals;
Limited public participation and transparency, with minimal influence from local communities, civil society, and marginalized groups;
Weak regulatory oversight, allowing vested economic and political interests to shape energy decisions with limited accountability.

content.text: To analyze how countries govern their energy transitions, the UNDP developed a conceptual framework that integrates governance principles with key elements of energy transition. The framework seeks to answer two critical questions:

content.title: How do countries use governance mechanisms to manage their energy transitions? (Governance needs)
How do energy transitions reshape governance structures? (Governance implications)

content.text:
To evaluate the effectiveness of the Just Energy Transition Governance Framework, the application of this conceptual framework was tested its application in Nigeria.

Note: It is important to note that the below content is not yet a case study but simply paraphrases and summarizes contributions that were shared by participants of the initial group conversations in Nigeria. These contributions are not analyzed or contextualized and represent the views of the individual interlocutors. The purpose of sharing this ‘raw material’ is to illustrate what discussions the conceptual framework proposed here can trigger.

The objective was to assess how governance mechanisms influence Nigeria’s energy transition policies, identify key challenges, and gather insights for refining the framework before applying it to other case studies.

Green Zones: Areas of Relative Readiness
Finance and Infrastructure: Stakeholders expressed some confidence in mobilizing investment, primarily through donor-supported mechanisms and public-private partnerships 💬️.

The application of the UNDP Just Energy Transition Governance Framework in Nigeria revealed several key insights into how governance structures shape, enable, or hinder a fair energy transition. These insights move beyond the existence of plans or laws, focusing instead on the operational dynamics of institutions, political leadership, participation, and accountability (UNDP, 2023).

Application and Findings:
1. From Policy Existence to Governance Effectiveness
One of the clearest takeaways was the distinction between having a policy and effectively implementing it. Although Nigeria has developed a forward-looking Energy Transition Plan (ETP), its execution has been constrained by fragmented mandates, siloed operations among ministries, and a lack of strategic alignment. The Energy Transition Office, for instance, shifted institutional homes, weakening continuity and long-term ownership.

The heat map color-coded matrix intersections were based on the number and intensity of stakeholder comments:
Red = High concern/frequent mentions
Yellow = Moderate concern/modest discussion
Green = Low concern/few comments
Red Zones: Areas of Critical Weakness
Political Vision and Inclusive Institutions: Poor inter-ministerial coordination, short-term thinking, and fragmented leadership. The transfer of the Energy Transition Office from the Vice President’s office to the National Climate Change Council weakened strategy cohesion.
Political Vision and Legal Frameworks: Conflicting policies, such as the expansion of gas in the face of net-zero goals, highlighted a lack of coherence. Stakeholders raised issues of regulatory capture and weak enforcement.
Political Vision and Civic Engagement: The ETP was initially developed by external consultants with limited civic input, particularly from women, youth, and rural communities.
Yellow Zones: Areas with Moderate Concern
Social Impacts and Legal Frameworks: There were inadequate policies for reskilling and social protection 💬️, as well as a lack of gender-disaggregated data.
Infrastructure and Innovation: While planning is underway, mechanisms for oversight and transparency remain weak.
UNDP Nigeria and its partners adopted a two-phase process to localize and test the framework:

content.title: Phase 1
content.body: Stakeholder mapping and desk review of Nigeria’s ETP, Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and the Electricity Act.

content.title: Phase 2
content.body: Group consultations with 29 stakeholders, including representatives from federal ministries, civil society, academia, and multilateral organizations, to identify and prioritize governance challenges.

content.text: Each contribution, whether an insight, concern, or proposal, was coded and categorized across the 16 matrix intersections, generating a Governance Heat Map below: (UNDP, 2023).

2. Subnational Participation
Given Nigeria’s federal structure and regional energy disparities, participants stressed the importance of involving state governments, local councils, and regional institutions. Doing so will require tailored facilitation strategies, multilingual materials, and training in governance tools.
3. Adding Quantitative Indicators
While the heat map provided a powerful qualitative snapshot, participants suggested complementing it with measurable indicators, such as:
Number of community consultations per state
Share of clean energy budget reaching local governments
The time between policy announcements and implementation
Court rulings on regulatory non-compliance
These metrics would help institutionalize monitoring and create feedback loops for adaptive governance.

2. Inclusive and Early Stakeholder Engagement
Effective deployment of the framework depends on involving stakeholders at an early stage. In Nigeria, this included government, civil society, academia, and the private sector. However, it was also noted that women’s groups, youth coalitions, and rural constituencies were underrepresented, underscoring the need for more deliberate outreach strategies.
3. Integration into Existing Policy Instruments
To have a lasting impact, governance findings should inform national processes such as budget cycles, policy revisions, or legislative reviews. In Nigeria, some inter-ministerial committees began using heat map insights to restructure coordination mechanisms under the new Electricity Act. Codifying this kind of uptake will be essential for institutional learning.
Areas for Strengthening:
1. Gender-Responsive Governance
Future applications of the framework should incorporate gender-specific governance metrics to enhance its effectiveness. This could include gender budgeting in transition finance, gender balance in decision-making bodies, and systematic collection of sex-disaggregated data 💬️. Strengthening the role of national women’s machineries in transition governance could enhance both legitimacy and equity.

5. The Heat Map as a Tool for Dialogue and Accountability
Participants valued the heat map not just as a technical diagnostic but as a participatory tool that enabled joint problem definition. It visually consolidated where governance was strong, weak, or ambiguous and encouraged different actors, ministries, civil society, and donors to speak the same language. It moved the conversation from general dissatisfaction to specific, actionable gaps.

Based on Nigeria’s experience, several lessons can inform how the UNDP governance framework might be adapted or scaled in other country contexts, especially where governance complexity intersects with the urgency of transition.
Conditions for Success:
1. Political Leadership and Mandate Clarity
Gaining traction with the framework requires more than technical engagement. Where political buy-in exists, such as through the Energy Transition Implementation Working Group or oversight by the National Climate Change Council, governance diagnostics can lead to real institutional change. Without this level of support, findings may not translate into action.

2. Social Equity Is a Structural Governance Issue
Equity concerns, particularly those related to gender, youth, and rural inclusion, emerged repeatedly. Participants noted that the ETP was largely gender-blind, lacked community participation during development, and offered limited pathways for affected groups to influence outcomes. These are not just policy omissions but reflections of how governance structures exclude certain groups from shaping national priorities.
3. Legal and Institutional Fragmentation
The consultations highlighted confusion and overlap between various government bodies involved in energy governance, including the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), the Rural Electrification Agency (REA), and ministries responsible for power, finance, and the environment. The absence of a coordinated legal and institutional framework leads to inefficiencies, conflicting actions, and a lack of accountability.
4. Civic Engagement Remains Ad Hoc
While some consultations occurred during updates to Nigeria’s nationally determined contributions 💬️ (NDCs), broader civic participation in energy policy remains ad hoc and non-institutionalized. Civil society groups expressed frustration over not being engaged in a structured and continuous manner, especially at the subnational level. This erodes the legitimacy of policies and hinders their responsiveness to local realities.

content.title: Case Study: Nigeria
content.subtitle: A Conceptual Framework for Just Energy Transition Governance

takeaways.title: Energy governance comprises the mechanisms, processes, policies, and institutions through which governments, people, communities, and corporations articulate their interests, exercise their legal rights, meet their obligations, and mediate their differences in relation to energy.

Governance systems must prioritize integrity, transparency, and independent oversight to build trust and ensure responsible decision-making. Mechanisms like independent audits and regulatory agencies are essential to evaluate and uphold accountability during energy transitions.
A just energy transition prioritieses Inclusive and effective institutions, legal and regulatory frameworks, civic engagement and empowerment and appropriate and independent oversight.
